claim: Msn2 and Msn4 function as master transcriptional regulators of yeast glycolysis via directly binding and activating genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
source: Here, we show that general stress response factors, Msn2 and Msn4, function as master transcriptional regulators of yeast glycolysis via directly binding and activating genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing Msn2/4 binding to glycolytic genes and RNA-seq data showing reduced expression of these genes in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants.

claim: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit prevalent repression of glycolytic genes.
source: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit prevalent repression of glycolytic genes and a significant delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation and reentry into growth from quiescence.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq showing down-regulation of glycolytic genes in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants.

claim: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit a significant delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation.
source: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit prevalent repression of glycolytic genes and a significant delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation and reentry into growth from quiescence.
evidence: Supported by acetyl-CoA measurements showing delayed accumulation in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants.

claim: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit a significant delay of reentry into growth from quiescence.
source: Yeast cells lacking Msn2 and Msn4 exhibit prevalent repression of glycolytic genes and a significant delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation and reentry into growth from quiescence.
evidence: Demonstrated by YMC oscillation data showing lengthened RC phase in mutants.

claim: Msn2/4 exhibit a dual role in activating carbohydrate metabolism genes and stress response genes.
source: Thus Msn2/4 exhibit a dual role in activating carbohydrate metabolism genes and stress response genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing Msn2/4 binding and regulation of both gene classes.

claim: Starvation-induced stress response factors may prime quiescent cells to reenter growth through glycolysis when nutrients are limited.
source: These results suggest a possible mechanism by which starvation-induced stress response factors may prime quiescent cells to reenter growth through glycolysis when nutrients are limited.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed role of Msn2/4 in regulating glycolysis and the transition from quiescence to growth.

claim: Acetyl-CoA stimulates cell growth under nutrient-limiting conditions.
source: Acetyl-CoA stimulates cell growth under nutrient-limiting conditions, but how cells generate acetyl-CoA under starvation stress is less understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Cai et al., 2011).

claim: When nutrients are limited, cells enter into quiescent states to enhance survival.
source: When nutrients are limited, cells enter into quiescent states to enhance survival (Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gray et al., 2004.

claim: Repletion of nutrients stimulates quiescent cells back into growth.
source: Repletion of nutrients stimulates quiescent cells back into growth (Dechant and Peter, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dechant and Peter, 2008.

claim: Gene expression and metabolite profiles are dramatically remodeled during the transitions between quiescence and growth.
source: Gene expression and metabolite profiles are dramatically remodeled during the transitions between quiescence and growth (Klosinska et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klosinska et al., 2011.

claim: In the YMC, cells are synchronized and exhibit respiratory oscillations under continuous, glucose-limited condition.
source: In the YMC, cells are synchronized and exhibit respiratory oscillations under continuous, glucose-limited condition (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2005; Tu et al., 2007 and Figure 1A showing oscillations.

claim: Thousands of transcripts and hundreds of metabolites are cycling as a function of the oxygen consumption oscillations in the YMC.
source: Thousands of transcripts and hundreds of metabolites are cycling as a function of the oxygen consumption oscillations, which divides the YMC into three phases: oxidative (OX), reductive building (RB) and reductive charging (RC).
evidence: Based on previous characterization of the YMC.

claim: In the OX phase, respiration peaks and growth genes including ribosomal and amino acid biosynthetic genes are activated.
source: In the OX phase, respiration peaks and growth genes including ribosomal and amino acid biosynthetic genes are activated.
evidence: Based on previous characterization of the YMC.

claim: Cell division occurs in the RB phase and cell cycle genes and mitochondrion genes are expressed.
source: Cell division occurs in the RB phase and cell cycle genes and mitochondrion genes are expressed.
evidence: Based on previous characterization of the YMC.

claim: The RC phase is associated with minimal respiration and genes associated with stress/survival responses, glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation are up-regulated.
source: The RC phase is associated with minimal respiration and genes associated with stress/survival responses, glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation are up-regulated.
evidence: Based on previous characterization of the YMC.

claim: RC phase cells exhibit stationary and quiescent characteristics including increased cell density, accumulation of storage carbohydrates glycogen and trehalose and expression of stationary specific genes.
source: RC phase cells exhibit stationary and quiescent characteristics including increased cell density, accumulation of storage carbohydrates glycogen and trehalose and expression of stationary specific genes (Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2010.

claim: The YMC can be viewed as consecutive alternations of growth, proliferation and quiescent phases.
source: Therefore, the YMC can be viewed as consecutive alternations of growth, proliferation and quiescent phases.
evidence: Based on inference from the characteristics of the three phases.

claim: Acetyl-CoA has been shown to drive the transition from RC/quiescence to OX/growth and RB/proliferation phase via the acetylation of histones at growth genes and G1 cyclin CLN3.
source: Acetyl-CoA has been shown to drive the transition from RC/quiescence to OX/growth and RB/proliferation phase via the acetylation of histones at growth genes and G1 cyclin CLN3 (Cai et al., 2011; Shi and Tu, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cai et al., 2011 and Shi and Tu, 2013.

claim: The role of promoting growth and proliferation by acetyl-CoA has been shown in various mammalian systems including embryonic stem cells and cancer cells.
source: The role of promoting growth and proliferation by acetyl-CoA has further been shown in various mammalian systems including embryonic stem cells and cancer cells (Comerford et al., 2014; Moussaieff et al., 2015; Sutendra et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Comerford et al., 2014; Moussaieff et al., 2015; Sutendra et al., 2014.

claim: DynaMO identified 41 TFs that were specifically linked to each of the three phases in the YMC.
source: We identified 41 TFs that were specifically linked to each of the three phases in the YMC.
evidence: Based on computational analysis using DynaMO algorithm.

claim: Msn2 and Msn4 are known to regulate the general stress response in budding yeast, including starvation, thermal, osmotic and oxidative stresses.
source: They are known to regulate the general stress response in budding yeast, including starvation, thermal, osmotic and oxidative stresses (Estruch and Carlson, 1993; Estruch, 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estruch and Carlson, 1993; Estruch, 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996.

claim: Deleting Msn2 and Msn4 caused a striking delay of transition from RC/quiescence to OX/growth phase in the YMC.
source: Deleting the two TFs caused a striking delay of transition from RC/quiescence to OX/growth phase in the YMC and slow accumulation of acetyl-CoA.
evidence: Demonstrated by YMC oscillation data in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants.

claim: Deleting Msn2 and Msn4 caused slow accumulation of acetyl-CoA.
source: Deleting the two TFs caused a striking delay of transition from RC/quiescence to OX/growth phase in the YMC and slow accumulation of acetyl-CoA.
evidence: Demonstrated by acetyl-CoA measurements in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants.

claim: Histone modification marks transcription regulatory regions and the intensity and dynamic nature of some modifications, such as H3K9ac correlates strongly with transcription activity.
source: Histone modification marks transcription regulatory regions and the intensity and dynamic nature of some modifications, such as H3K9ac correlates strongly with transcription activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Three temporal binding patterns were captured in the YMC, consistent with the three metabolic phases.
source: Three temporal binding patterns were captured, consistent with the three metabolic phases of the YMC (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by clustering analysis of H3K9ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The functions of the 41 candidate TFs were consistent with the transcriptional diagram in each phase.
source: In general, the functions of these candidate TFs were consistent with the transcriptional diagram in each phase (Kuang et al., 2017), such as ribosome biogenesis TFs Rap1 and Sfp1 enriched in cluster 1 (OX/growth), cell cycle TFs Mbp1 and Swi6 enriched in cluster 2 (RB/proliferation), and stress response TFs Msn2 and Msn4 enriched in cluster 3 (RC/quiescence) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis and known functions of TFs.

claim: Validation experiments showed a significantly higher frequency of disrupted YMC oscillation in the candidate TFs than in control randomly selected TFs.
source: Validation experiments performed by mutating individual TFs also show a significantly higher frequency of disrupted YMC oscillation (as measured by O2 consumption) in the candidate TFs (Arg80, Gcr1, Xbp1, Msn2, Msn4) than in control randomly selected TFs (Skn7, Arg81, Oaf1, Cin5, Ume6).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental validation of TF mutants.

claim: The msn2Δ mutant showed a 'lengthened RC phase' phenotype where the RC phase is longer than that in the WT strain and it gets longer after each cycle.
source: From the validation experiments, we observed a very unusual and specific 'lengthened RC phase' phenotype in the msn2Δ mutant (Figure 2A). The RC phase is longer than that in the WT strain and it gets longer after each cycle.
evidence: Demonstrated by YMC oscillation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: msn2Δmsn4Δ showed a more severe defect than msn2Δ whereas msn4Δ was relatively normal, in support of partial functional redundancy.
source: msn2Δmsn4Δ showed a more severe defect than msn2Δ whereas msn4Δ was relatively normal, in support of partial functional redundancy in this instance (Estruch, 2000).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of YMC oscillation phenotypes in different mutants.

claim: Some genes are completely turned off in the msn2Δ single mutant while other genes show reduced expression in the msn2Δ single mutant and are completely eliminated in the double mutant.
source: This may be consistent with previous observations that some genes are completely turned off in the msn2Δ single mutant while other genes show reduced expression in the msn2Δ single mutant and are completely eliminated in the double mutant (Estruch, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Estruch, 2000.

claim: The timing of the OX/growth and RB/proliferation phases is normal in the msn2Δmsn4Δ mutants but the RC/quiescence phase is seemingly ever-lengthening.
source: The timing of the OX/growth and RB/proliferation phases is normal in the mutants but the RC/quiescence phase is seemingly ever-lengthening, as though the cells await an ever-diminishing signal to proceed.
evidence: Inferred from YMC oscillation data.

claim: Many stress response genes known to be the targets of Msn2/4 are activated in the RC phase.
source: First, many stress response genes known to be the targets of Msn2/4 are activated in the RC phase (Gasch et al., 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gasch et al., 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996.

claim: Msn2/Msn4 motif sites were enriched in the predicted RC phase binding sites.
source: Second, Msn2/Msn4 motif sites were enriched in the predicted RC phase binding sites (Figure 1B, cluster 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by DynaMO analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MSN4 mRNA level is increased in the RC phase while MSN2 mRNA level is relatively constant.
source: MSN4 mRNA level is increased in the RC phase while MSN2 mRNA level is relatively constant (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MSN4 expression is activated by stress but MSN2 is constitutively expressed.
source: This is in line with previous findings that MSN4 expression is activated by stress but MSN2 is constitutively expressed (Gasch et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gasch et al., 2000.

claim: Both Msn2 and Msn4 showed increased binding to the genome in the RC/quiescence phase.
source: Both TFs showed increased binding to the genome in the RC/quiescence phase regionally (Figure 2C) and genome-wide (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Msn2 and Msn4 shared a significant proportion of binding sites and target genes.
source: Msn2 and Msn4 shared a significant proportion of binding sites and target genes (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), supporting their largely redundant functions.
evidence: Demonstrated by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A substantial proportion of Msn2/4 target genes are expressed in the RC phase.
source: Among the targets of Msn2 and Msn4, we observed a substantial proportion of genes expressed in the RC phase (Figure 2F), further supporting the hypothesis that Msn2/4 function in RC phase.
evidence: Demonstrated by GO term analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Msn2/4 target genes are enriched in classes of carbohydrate metabolism.
source: Additionally, Msn2/4 target genes are enriched in classes of carbohydrate metabolism (Figure 2F), indicating that Msn2/4 may function through remodeling the metabolic pathways.
evidence: Demonstrated by GO term analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Acetate can directly induce an OX phase when added in the RC phase.
source: Cai et al. (Cai et al., 2011) showed that adding acetate in the RC phase can directly induce an OX phase and they found that acetyl-CoA is the key metabolite that initiates cell growth and proliferation by promoting histone acetylation at growth genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2011.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is the key metabolite that initiates cell growth and proliferation by promoting histone acetylation at growth genes.
source: Cai et al. (Cai et al., 2011) showed that adding acetate in the RC phase can directly induce an OX phase and they found that acetyl-CoA is the key metabolite that initiates cell growth and proliferation by promoting histone acetylation at growth genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2011.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is low at the beginning of RC phase and it is accumulated during the RC phase.
source: Acetyl-CoA is low at the beginning of RC phase and it is accumulated during the RC phase. When it reaches a threshold, it initiates the cell growth program.
evidence: Based on previous work and inference.

claim: When acetyl-CoA reaches a threshold, it initiates the cell growth program.
source: Acetyl-CoA is low at the beginning of RC phase and it is accumulated during the RC phase. When it reaches a threshold, it initiates the cell growth program.
evidence: Based on previous work and inference.

claim: Acetate can efficiently stimulate the OX phase in msn2Δ mutant no matter when in the RC phase acetate was added.
source: Although the RC phase is much longer in the mutant than that in the WT, acetate still stimulated the OX phase efficiently no matter when in the RC phase acetate was added (Figure 3A), consistent with the possibility that acetate or acetyl-CoA represented the limiting factor.
evidence: Demonstrated by acetate addition experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Similar results of acetate-induced OX phase were observed in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant.
source: Similar results were observed in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant.
evidence: Demonstrated by acetate addition experiments.

claim: Msn2 and Msn4 might be involved in nutrient signaling, perhaps based on the accumulating intracellular acetyl-CoA level.
source: The observations suggested that Msn2 and Msn4 might be involved in nutrient signaling, perhaps based on the accumulating intracellular acetyl-CoA level.
evidence: Based on inference from acetate addition experiments.

claim: There is a dramatic delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant cells.
source: We measured acetyl-CoA levels in WT and mutant cells and observed a dramatic delay of acetyl-CoA accumulation in the mutant cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by acetyl-CoA measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Msn2/4 control the transition from RC to OX phase by regulating the accumulation of acetyl-CoA.
source: Together, the results suggested that Msn2/4 control the transition from RC to OX phase by regulating the accumulation of acetyl-CoA.
evidence: Based on inference from acetyl-CoA measurements and YMC phenotypes.

claim: Glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation are the major carbon metabolic pathways activated in the RC phase.
source: Glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation are the major carbon metabolic pathways activated in the RC phase (Figure 1A) (Tu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2005 and Figure 1A.

claim: 20 of the 33 genes encoding glycolytic enzymes were predicted to be bound by Msn2/4.
source: DynaMO prediction analysis indicated that 20 of the 33 genes encoding glycolytic enzymes were predicted to be bound by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D) and the number of predicted binding sites was significantly higher than the number of sites from random sets of genes (p<1×10−5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by DynaMO analysis shown in Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The number of predicted Msn2/4 binding sites at glycolytic genes was significantly higher than the number of sites from random sets of genes (p<1×10−5).
source: DynaMO prediction analysis indicated that 20 of the 33 genes encoding glycolytic enzymes were predicted to be bound by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D) and the number of predicted binding sites was significantly higher than the number of sites from random sets of genes (p<1×10−5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: 27 out of the 33 genes encoding glycolytic enzymes were bound by Msn2/4.
source: We confirmed the observation by examining the ChIP-seq results. 27 out of the 33 genes were bound by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and intriguingly, binding of Msn2/4 extends into the coding regions for some of the genes, which may suggest some unknown regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Binding of Msn2/4 extends into the coding regions for some of the glycolytic genes.
source: We confirmed the observation by examining the ChIP-seq results. 27 out of the 33 genes were bound by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and intriguingly, binding of Msn2/4 extends into the coding regions for some of the genes, which may suggest some unknown regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The coding regions of glycolytic genes are more conserved than the coding regions of other genes.
source: The coding regions of glycolytic genes are more conserved than the coding regions of other genes and the promoter regions of glycolytic genes in Saccaromyces strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The coding regions of glycolytic genes are more conserved than the promoter regions of glycolytic genes in Saccaromyces strains.
source: The coding regions of glycolytic genes are more conserved than the coding regions of other genes and the promoter regions of glycolytic genes in Saccaromyces strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of motif sites overlapping Msn2/4 peaks at glycolytic genes was significantly higher than the number of sites from random sets of 33 genes (p<1×10−7).
source: The number of motif sites overlapping Msn2/4 peaks was significantly higher than the number of sites from random sets of 33 genes (p<1×10−7; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,F.

claim: Only 2 of 11 genes encoding enzymes in fatty acid oxidation were bound by Msn2/4.
source: On the other hand, only 2 of 11 genes encoding enzymes in fatty acid oxidation were bound by Msn2/4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Glycolytic genes were highly induced in the WT cells during the RC phase but were dramatically reduced in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant.
source: These genes were highly induced in the WT cells during the RC phase but were surprisingly dramatically reduced in the mutant (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Msn2 and Msn4 control the transition from RC/quiescent state to OX/growth state by regulating the intracellular level of acetyl-CoA through glycolysis.
source: Collectively, the results suggest that Msn2 and Msn4 control the transition from RC/quiescent state to OX/growth state by regulating the intracellular level of acetyl-CoA through glycolysis.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and acetyl-CoA measurements.

claim: The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex was not targeted by Msn2/4.
source: Although we lack direct evidence for which intracellular pool of acetyl-CoA is regulated by Msn2/4, the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which functions in mitochondria, was not targeted by Msn2/4, whereas multiple cytosolic enzymes were targeted by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the nucleo-cytosolic pool of acetyl-CoA might be specifically regulated.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Multiple cytosolic enzymes were targeted by Msn2/4.
source: Although we lack direct evidence for which intracellular pool of acetyl-CoA is regulated by Msn2/4, the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which functions in mitochondria, was not targeted by Msn2/4, whereas multiple cytosolic enzymes were targeted by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the nucleo-cytosolic pool of acetyl-CoA might be specifically regulated.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The nucleo-cytosolic pool of acetyl-CoA might be specifically regulated by Msn2/4.
source: Although we lack direct evidence for which intracellular pool of acetyl-CoA is regulated by Msn2/4, the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which functions in mitochondria, was not targeted by Msn2/4, whereas multiple cytosolic enzymes were targeted by Msn2/4 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the nucleo-cytosolic pool of acetyl-CoA might be specifically regulated.
evidence: Based on inference from ChIP-seq data showing targeting of cytosolic but not mitochondrial enzymes.

claim: Acetate, ethanol and acetaldehyde can induce the transition from RC to OX.
source: It is also consistent with two other lines of previously obtained evidence: (1) that acetate, ethanol and acetaldehyde can induce the transition from RC to OX and (2) that histone acetylation is dramatically increased during such transitions (Cai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2011.

claim: Histone acetylation is dramatically increased during transitions from RC to OX.
source: It is also consistent with two other lines of previously obtained evidence: (1) that acetate, ethanol and acetaldehyde can induce the transition from RC to OX and (2) that histone acetylation is dramatically increased during such transitions (Cai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2011.

claim: The oncogene MYC similarly regulates glycolytic genes in mammals.
source: Interestingly, the oncogene MYC similarly regulates glycolytic genes in mammals (Dang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dang, 2012.

claim: There is a delay of growth in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant compared to the WT strain when 6 day stationary phase cells are added into fresh YPD medium.
source: Interestingly, we still observed a delay of growth in the msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant compared to the WT strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Inoculation in YP +2% galactose exhibited a bigger delay in growth for msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant, probably because Msn2/4 also control the expression of genes in the galactose metabolism pathway.
source: Inoculation in YP +2% galactose exhibited a bigger delay, probably because Msn2/4 also control the expression of genes in the galactose metabolism pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and pathway analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant showed a much lower saturation titer compared to the WT.
source: The msn2Δmsn4Δ double mutant also showed a much lower saturation titer compared to the WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Deletion of MSN2 and MSN4 did not affect survival rate in glucose medium.
source: Deletion of MSN2 and MSN4 did not affect survival rate in glucose medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) but decreased the size of stationary cells in glucose medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival rate measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Deletion of MSN2 and MSN4 decreased the size of stationary cells in glucose medium.
source: Deletion of MSN2 and MSN4 did not affect survival rate in glucose medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) but decreased the size of stationary cells in glucose medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The three clusters of gene expression patterns (OX, RB, RC) were still observed in the msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant cells.
source: The three clusters of gene expression patterns were still observed in the mutant cells. However, many RC genes were clearly down-regulated.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Many RC genes were clearly down-regulated in the msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant cells.
source: The three clusters of gene expression patterns were still observed in the mutant cells. However, many RC genes were clearly down-regulated.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 366 genes were up-regulated and 426 genes were down-regulated in msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant compared to WT cells at comparable time points.
source: Next, we identified 366 genes up-regulated and 426 genes down-regulated in mutant compared to WT cells at comparable time points.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: The 366 up-regulated genes were relatively equally distributed among OX, RB, RC and non-cycling groups.
source: Whereas the 366 up-regulated genes were relatively equally distributed among OX, RB, RC and non-cycling groups, the majority (62.2%) of the 426 down-regulated genes were RC phase genes (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The majority (62.2%) of the 426 down-regulated genes were RC phase genes.
source: Whereas the 366 up-regulated genes were relatively equally distributed among OX, RB, RC and non-cycling groups, the majority (62.2%) of the 426 down-regulated genes were RC phase genes (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For both up-regulated and down-regulated genes, the changes were primarily observed in the RC phase.
source: For both up-regulated and down-regulated genes, the changes were primarily observed in the RC phase (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Among the down-regulated genes, there is significant enrichment of genes related to carbohydrate metabolism and response to various stresses.
source: Among these genes, we found significant enrichment of genes related to carbohydrate metabolism and response to various stresses (Figure 4B), and the GO terms were very similar to those detected by ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by GO term analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FAA1 and POX1, which are directly involved in fatty acid β-oxidation and bound by Msn2/4, did not show significant changes of mRNA level in the mutant cells.
source: FAA1 and POX1, which are directly involved in fatty acid β-oxidation and bound by Msn2/4, did not show significant changes of mRNA level in the mutant cells (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The lack of change in FAA1 and POX1 expression argues against the hypothesis that Msn2/4 promote acetyl-CoA production through fatty acid oxidation.
source: This argues against the hypothesis that Msn2/4 promote acetyl-CoA production through fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: Based on inference from RNA-seq data.

claim: 112 genes appear to be repressed by Msn2/4 in WT cells (transcripts are up in mutant cells).
source: 112 genes, including 27 OX, 40 RB, 22 RC and 23 non-cycling genes, appear to be repressed by Msn2/4 in WT cells (Figure 4C; transcripts are up in mutant cells).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of 'core' targets shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 136 genes appear to be directly activated by Msn2/4 in WT cells (Down in mutant cells).
source: 136 genes appear to be directly activated by Msn2/4 in WT cells (i.e., Down in mutant cells) and more than half of them (81 genes) were RC phase genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of 'core' targets shown in Figure 4C.

claim: More than half (81 genes) of the 136 genes activated by Msn2/4 were RC phase genes.
source: 136 genes appear to be directly activated by Msn2/4 in WT cells (i.e., Down in mutant cells) and more than half of them (81 genes) were RC phase genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of 'core' targets shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The timing of Msn2/4 binding is consistent with their activating function for target RC phase genes.
source: The timing of Msn2/4 binding is consistent with their activating function for target RC phase genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by temporal analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Carbohydrate metabolism genes and stress response genes are the two major classes in the core Msn2/4 targets.
source: Carbohydrate metabolism genes and stress response genes are the two major classes in the core Msn2/4 targets (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Many genes encoding glycolytic enzymes, such as HXK1, GLK1, ENO1, ENO2, PGK1, GPM1, TDH1 and TDH3 are core Msn2/4 targets.
source: As shown previously, many genes encoding glycolytic enzymes, such as HXK1, GLK1, ENO1, ENO2, PGK1, GPM1, TDH1 and TDH3 are core Msn2/4 targets.
evidence: Demonstrated by combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Heat-shock protein genes such as HSP12, HSP26, HSP78 and HSP82 are core Msn2/4 targets.
source: Heat-shock protein genes such as HSP12, HSP26, HSP78 and HSP82, oxidative stress response genes including CTT1, PRX1, SOD1, SOD2 are also core Msn2/4 targets.
evidence: Demonstrated by combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Oxidative stress response genes including CTT1, PRX1, SOD1, SOD2 are core Msn2/4 targets.
source: Heat-shock protein genes such as HSP12, HSP26, HSP78 and HSP82, oxidative stress response genes including CTT1, PRX1, SOD1, SOD2 are also core Msn2/4 targets.
evidence: Demonstrated by combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: TPS2 and GAC1, which are involved in the synthesis of trehalose and glycogen, are important for stress response.
source: For example, TPS2 and GAC1, which are involved in the synthesis of trehalose and glycogen, two storage carbohydrates, are important for stress response.
evidence: Based on established knowledge.

claim: Trehalose and glycogen have been shown to be metabolized during the exit of quiescence to fuel the regrowth.
source: Interestingly, trehalose and glycogen have also been shown to be metabolized during the exit of quiescence to fuel the regrowth (Shi et al., 2010; Silljé et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi et al., 2010 and Silljé et al., 1999.

claim: Msn2/4 may facilitate the metabolism of trehalose and glycogen during exit from quiescence by activating NTH1, ATH1, GPH1, PGM1 and PGM2.
source: Msn2/4 may also facilitate these processes by activating NTH1, ATH1, GPH1, PGM1 and PGM2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on inference from ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The regulatory network for Msn2/4 suggests parallel mechanisms for how yeast responds to limited nutrients.
source: Therefore, the regulatory network for Msn2/4 suggests parallel mechanisms for how yeast responds to limited nutrients.
evidence: Based on inference from the regulatory network analysis.

claim: Stress response genes are activated to maintain survival by removing detrimental factors like mis-folded proteins and oxygen radicals and improving defenses.
source: Stress response genes are activated to maintain survival by removing detrimental factors like mis-folded proteins and oxygen radicals and improving defenses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of stress response.

claim: Carbohydrate metabolism genes are activated so that cells can utilize the very limited nutrients in the environment for growth during recovery from quiescence.
source: Carbohydrate metabolism genes are also activated so that cells can utilize the very limited nutrients in the environment for growth, as may often be the case in recovery from quiescence.
evidence: Based on inference from the regulatory network analysis.

claim: The majority of the OX/growth genes, which function in biomass synthesis, are turned off when nutrients are scarce.
source: The majority of the OX/growth genes, which function in biomass synthesis, are turned off when nutrients are scarce, as are the cell cycle genes which peak in the RB/proliferation phase.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of gene expression in YMC and nutrient-scarce conditions.

claim: Cell cycle genes which peak in the RB/proliferation phase are turned off when nutrients are scarce.
source: The majority of the OX/growth genes, which function in biomass synthesis, are turned off when nutrients are scarce, as are the cell cycle genes which peak in the RB/proliferation phase.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of gene expression in YMC and nutrient-scarce conditions.

claim: Mitochondrial genes, which peak in the RB phase, are relatively elevated upon nutrient scarcity.
source: Interestingly, mitochondrial genes, which also peak in the RB phase, are relatively elevated upon nutrient scarcity.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of gene expression in YMC and nutrient-scarce conditions.

claim: Genes encoding mitochondrial ribosome components are induced temporally at the beginning of glucose starvation or phosphate limitation but not under other conditions.
source: Genes encoding mitochondrial ribosome components are induced temporally at the beginning of glucose starvation or phosphate limitation but not under other conditions while genes encoding translation factors are activated modestly across all nutrient scarce conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes encoding translation factors are activated modestly across all nutrient scarce conditions.
source: Genes encoding mitochondrial ribosome components are induced temporally at the beginning of glucose starvation or phosphate limitation but not under other conditions while genes encoding translation factors are activated modestly across all nutrient scarce conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most RC genes are induced under nutrient scarce conditions, reflecting the similarity between the RC phase and other quiescent states.
source: Not surprisingly, most RC genes are induced under nutrient scarce conditions too, reflecting the similarity between the RC phase and other quiescent states.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of gene expression in YMC and nutrient-scarce conditions.

claim: The majority of genes encoding glycolytic enzymes are expressed in the RC phase.
source: We specifically examined genes encoding glycolytic enzymes, most of which are expressed in the RC phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The majority of genes encoding glycolytic enzymes are turned on under nutrient starvation or limitation conditions.
source: The majority of these genes are also turned on under nutrient starvation or limitation conditions, suggesting a signal importance of in quiescent states.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of gene expression in YMC and nutrient-scarce conditions.

claim: Most previous studies on Msn2/4 were performed under various stress conditions such as starvation, heat shock, osmotic and oxidative stresses and used cell viability as readout.
source: Most previous studies on Msn2/4 were performed under various stress conditions such as starvation, heat shock, osmotic and oxidative stresses and used cell viability as readout (Estruch and Carlson, 1993; Estruch, 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estruch and Carlson, 1993; Estruch, 2000; Martínez-Pastor et al., 1996; Schmitt and McEntee, 1996.

claim: In the YMC, in which nutrient is continuously limited, growth, proliferation and quiescence are temporally separated, providing a platform for mechanistic exploration of transitions between distinct cellular states.
source: In the YMC, in which nutrient is continuously limited, growth, proliferation and quiescence are temporally separated, providing a platform for mechanistic exploration of transitions between distinct cellular states.
evidence: Based on the characteristics of the YMC system.

claim: The unusual 'lengthened RC phase' phenotype in MSN2 and MSN4 mutants is consistent with a transcriptional program in the quiescent phase which could be critical for subsequent cell proliferation.
source: The unusual 'lengthened RC phase' phenotype in MSN2 and MSN4 mutants is consistent with a transcriptional program in the quiescent phase which could be critical for subsequent cell proliferation.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed phenotype.

claim: Msn2/4 modulate the cellular programs by changing the intracellular acetyl-CoA levels, probably by promoting glycolysis.
source: Our analyses suggest that Msn2/4 modulate the cellular programs by changing the intracellular acetyl-CoA levels, probably by promoting glycolysis.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Metabolism has strong effects on cell growth and proliferation.
source: Metabolism has strong effects on cell growth and proliferation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge.

claim: Metabolites such as acetyl-CoA function not only as building blocks for the synthesis of fatty acids, amino acids and nucleotides, but also as signals for gene expression and enzymatic activities.
source: Metabolites such as acetyl-CoA have been shown to function not only as building blocks for the synthesis of fatty acids, amino acids and nucleotides, but also as signals for gene expression and enzymatic activities (Lyssiotis and Cantley, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lyssiotis and Cantley, 2014.

claim: Acetyl-CoA has been proposed as a central metabolite that regulates cellular growth program from yeast to cancer cells.
source: Acetyl-CoA has been proposed as a central metabolite that regulates cellular growth program from yeast to cancer cells (Cai et al., 2011; Comerford et al., 2014; Mashimo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cai et al., 2011; Comerford et al., 2014; Mashimo et al., 2014.

claim: In budding yeast, transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4 function as key transcription factors that activate genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
source: Does a transcriptional program exist to control the acetyl-CoA level? Our analyses offer evidence that in budding yeast, transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4, well known as stress response factors, function as key transcription factors that activate genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: By controlling expression of glycolytic enzymes, Msn2/4 may support the generation of acetyl-CoA in preparation for cell growth and proliferation.
source: By controlling expression of these enzymes, Msn2/4 may support the generation of acetyl-CoA in preparation for cell growth and proliferation.
evidence: Based on inference from the regulatory role of Msn2/4.

claim: The regulatory mode of Msn2/4 is not obvious when cells are grown in rich medium, probably because acetyl-CoA level is high enough to support continuous growth.
source: This regulatory mode is not obvious when cells are grown in rich medium, probably because acetyl-CoA level is high enough to support continuous growth.
evidence: Based on inference and speculation.

claim: The regulatory mode of Msn2/4 becomes extremely important when cells are under nutrient-limited condition.
source: But it becomes extremely important when cells are under nutrient-limited condition.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed phenotypes under nutrient-limited conditions.

claim: Nutrient limitation is sensed by TOR signaling and inhibition of TORC1 leads to nuclear translocation and activation of Msn2/4 and other stress response TFs.
source: Supposedly, nutrient limitation is sensed by TOR signaling and inhibition of TORC1 leads to nuclear translocation and activation of Msn2/4 and other stress response TFs (Beck and Hall, 1999; Loewith and Hall, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beck and Hall, 1999 and Loewith and Hall, 2011.

claim: Many stress response TFs, such as Gis1, Mig1/2/3, and Msn2/4, that target metabolic enzymes were identified in the RC/quiescent phase of YMC by DynaMO.
source: That probably explains why many stress response TFs, such as Gis1, Mig1/2/3, and Msn2/4, that target metabolic enzymes were identified in the RC/quiescent phase of YMC by DynaMO (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by DynaMO analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: This study seemingly uncovers a critically important secondary mechanism for stress response – in the quiescent state, remodeling metabolic activities and activating stress responses and defenses pathways to maintain survival, and then enabling rapidly regrowth once nutrients are replenished.
source: Therefore, this study seemingly uncover a critically important secondary mechanism for stress response – in the quiescent state, remodeling metabolic activities and activating stress responses and defenses pathways to maintain survival, and then enabling rapidly regrowth once nutrients are replenished (Ho and Gasch, 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from the overall findings and supported by citation to Ho and Gasch, 2015.

claim: Msn2/4-dependent glycolysis potentially provides fuels supporting cell growth under continuous nutrient limited conditions, similar to the situation in cancers.
source: Msn2/4-dependent glycolysis potentially provides fuels supporting cell growth under continuous nutrient limited conditions, similar to the situation in cancers, which are also associated with robust glycolysis and survive under nutrient limited conditions (Comerford et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference and supported by citation to Comerford et al., 2014.

claim: Cancers are associated with robust glycolysis and survive under nutrient limited conditions.
source: Msn2/4-dependent glycolysis potentially provides fuels supporting cell growth under continuous nutrient limited conditions, similar to the situation in cancers, which are also associated with robust glycolysis and survive under nutrient limited conditions (Comerford et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Comerford et al., 2014.

claim: A functional equivalent of Msn2/4 in mammalian cancer is MYC, which similarly targets all glycolytic enzymes and fosters tumor growth.
source: One speculative hypothesis is that a functional equivalent of Msn2/4 in mammalian cancer is MYC, which similarly targets all glycolytic enzymes and fosters tumor growth (Dang, 2012).
evidence: Based on speculation and supported by citation to Dang, 2012.

claim: TF dependent activation of glycolysis to support cell proliferation under nutrient limited condition can be a prevalent biological motif.
source: It suggests that TF dependent activation of glycolysis to support cell proliferation under nutrient limited condition can be a prevalent biological motif.
evidence: Based on inference from the findings in yeast and comparison to mammalian systems.
